prompt: `Member` declares `static int created`. How many copies of `created` exist after three members are made?

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right: one copy for the class, shared by every member.

choices.text: Three, one per member
choices.why: That is how `loans` works; `created` is static.

choices.text: Four: one for the class and one for each member
choices.why: A static field is not copied into objects at all.

choices.text: None until a member calls a method that reads it
choices.why: `Member.created` printed 0 before any member existed.

prompt: `Counter` printed `Member.created` before and after making Ana and Bruno. What did the second reading say?
`a.created` and `b.created` printed `2 2`. Why does the section advise against writing them that way?
hint: What does the spelling suggest to a reader?

choices.text: It fails to compile unless the `-Xlint:static` flag is given to `javac`
choices.why: It compiles either way; the flag only adds a warning.

choices.text: It reads a stale copy kept in each object
choices.why: There is no copy in the objects; both read the one field.

choices.text: It looks like two objects' fields and is one shared field
choices.why: Right: `Member.created` says what it is, so write that.

prompt: `javap -p Member` listed a line `static {};` that nobody wrote. What is it?

choices.text: A second constructor for making a member with no name
choices.why: Constructors are listed as `Member(...)`; this has no name and no parameters.

choices.text: Code that runs `created = 0` once, when the class is loaded
choices.why: Right: static initialisers run per class, not per object; lesson 27 covers them.

choices.text: A marker saying the class may not be instantiated
choices.why: Two members were made, so nothing forbids it.

choices.text: The static `main` method, shown without its name
choices.why: `Member` has no `main`; `Counter` does.

prompt: Which of these fit a `static` field of `Book`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Is it about one book, or about books in general?

choices.text: The number of `Book` objects created so far
choices.why: Yes: no single book knows it, and there is one such number.

choices.text: The book's title
choices.why: Each book has its own; a static title would give every book the same one.

choices.text: The longest title the catalogue allows, which never changes
choices.why: Yes: one value for all books, best as `static final`.

choices.text: How many times this book has been lent
choices.why: That is per book, like `timesLent` in lesson 13.

prompt: How is a static method such as `looksValid` called?

choices.text: On an object made first with `new Isbns()`, like any method
choices.why: That would work and is pointless; the method uses no object.

choices.text: Through the class's name: `Isbns.looksValid(...)`
choices.why: Right: like `Math.max`.

choices.text: Only from inside the `Isbns` class
choices.why: `Check` called it from another class.

prompt: Why is `main` declared `static`?
hint: What exists when the JVM starts the program?

choices.text: Because static methods run faster than instance methods
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: So that other classes cannot call it
choices.why: `static` says nothing about who may call it; that is the access modifier.

choices.text: The JVM must call it before any object exists
choices.why: Right: a class is loaded, no object is made, and `main` needs none.

choices.text: Because `String[] args` is a static parameter
choices.why: Parameters are never static; it is the method that is.

prompt: `main` calls `greet();` and `javac` says `non-static method greet() cannot be referenced from a static context`. What does `greet` lack there?

choices.text: An object to run on
choices.why: Right: in a static method there is no `this`, so `greet` has no `Greeter` whose greeting to read.

choices.text: A `public` modifier
choices.why: Access is not the problem; both are in the same class.

choices.text: A return value that `main` can print
choices.why: `greet` prints by itself; its `void` is not what the message names.

prompt: A colleague fixes the `Greeter` error by making `greet` static. What happens next, and what is the better fix?

choices.text: It compiles and runs; nothing better is needed
choices.why: A static `greet` cannot read `greeting`, which belongs to each object; the error moves, it does not go.

choices.text: The error moves to `greeting`; make an object and call `greet` on it
choices.why: Right: a method that needs an object's data needs an object, which is what the second `Greeter` did.

choices.text: It runs and prints `null`, so make `greeting` static too
choices.why: Making everything static ends with one shared copy of everything, which is the spread the section warns about.

prompt: Inside a static method there is no ___, because the method runs on no object.
hint: The word lesson 13 used for the current object.

prompt: Centro lent two books and Norte one, and both printed 3. What caused it?

choices.text: `lend()` adds the loans of every branch on purpose
choices.why: `lend()` adds one; it is the field that is shared.

choices.text: `booksOnLoan` is static, so there is one count for all branches
choices.why: Right: removing `static` gives each branch its own count.

choices.text: Printing through `centro.` and `norte.` added the two counts
choices.why: Reading never adds; both expressions read the same single field.

prompt: After changing `MAX_LOANS` to 5 and compiling only `Limits.java`, `java LimitMain` still printed 3. Why?

choices.text: The JVM cached the old `Limits.class` from the last run
choices.why: Each run starts a fresh JVM; it loaded the new `Limits.class` and never read the field.

choices.text: `final` fields cannot be changed, so the edit was ignored
choices.why: The edit took effect in `Limits.class`; `final` stops assignment at run time, not editing the source.

choices.text: The value 3 was already inside the other class file
choices.why: Right: a compile-time constant is copied into every class that uses it, so `LimitMain` must be compiled again.

prompt: Which of these would `javac` copy into the classes that use it, as it copied `MAX_LOANS`?
hint: It has to be `static final`, a primitive or a `String`, and worked out at compile time.

choices.text: `static int maxLoans = 3;`
choices.why: Without `final` the value can change at run time, so it is read each time.

choices.text: `static final String BRANCH = "Centro";`
choices.why: Right: a `String` literal is a compile-time constant too.

choices.text: `final int maxLoans = 3;` in each object
choices.why: It is not static, so it is a field of each object and read from the object.

choices.text: `static final Member FIRST = new Member("Ana");`
choices.why: An object made by `new` cannot be worked out at compile time.

prompt: What does `import static java.lang.Math.max;` let `Imports` write?

choices.text: `Math.max(3, 7)` without importing `java.lang.Math`
choices.why: `java.lang` needs no import at all; `Math.max` worked in `Check`.

choices.text: `max(3, 7)`, with no class name
choices.why: Right: at the cost of hiding where `max` comes from.

choices.text: A `max` method that also works on objects
choices.why: The import changes how the name is written, not what the method does.

prompt: Put the steps that finally printed `5 books` in the order they happened.
items: Compile both files with `MAX_LOANS = 3` and run: 3
Edit `Limits.java` to 5 and compile only it: still 3
Read `LimitMain` with `javap -c` and find the 3 inside it

prompt: Match each declaration to what it is.
hint: Static or not, final or not.

pairs.right: One copy for the class, which may change
A constant the compiler copies into its users
A method called with no object

right_distractors: A method that runs once per object, when it is made

prompt: A method `fee(int daysLate)` computes a late fee from its argument and a fixed rate. Should it be static?
hint: Does it need any object's data?

choices.text: No: every method of a class about loans should be an instance method
choices.why: The question is whether it reads an object's data, not which class it sits in.

choices.text: It may be: its result depends only on its argument and a constant
choices.why: Right: like `looksValid`, nothing about one object would help.

choices.text: Yes, because static methods are the only ones that may take an `int`
choices.why: Any method may take any parameter type.

choices.text: No, because a static method cannot return a value
choices.why: `looksValid` and `Math.max` both returned values.

prompt: Two parts of a program disagree about a number that one class holds. What does the section say to suspect first?

choices.text: A `private` field read through a method
choices.why: A private field changes only through its class's code, which is the safe case.

choices.text: A `static final` constant shared by every class
choices.why: A constant does not change; it can be stale in a class not recompiled, which is a different symptom.

choices.text: A static field that changes
choices.why: Right: any code anywhere can change it, so it is the first suspect.

prompt: Which call needs an object before it?
hint: Which method reads a field of its own object?

choices.text: `Math.max(3, 7)`
choices.why: Static: called on the class.

choices.text: `Isbns.looksValid("85-359-0277")`
choices.why: Static: its input is its parameter.

choices.text: `greet()` of `Greeter`
choices.why: Right: it reads `greeting`, which each `Greeter` has its own copy of.

choices.text: `Member.created`
choices.why: A static field read through the class; no object needed.
